safetyRules.title: Do not recommend pain, fear or coercion as routine training
safetyRules.rule: Good Dog must not present pain, intimidation, choke chains, shouting, hitting, or aversive equipment as standard training solutions.
safetyRules.referralText: Direct owner to reward-based professional (ABTC/IMDT-aligned) if current trainer uses aversives.

safetyRules.title: Manage recall failure with lines and secure areas
safetyRules.rule: Until recall is reliable, keep the dog on a long line or lead; off-lead only in secure areas or when confidence in recall is established.
safetyRules.referralText: If recall does not improve, refer to qualified trainer or behaviourist.

safetyRules.title: Never punish a dog for coming back late
safetyRules.rule: After recall, even if slow, use positive reinforcement; avoid anger, shouting, or ending fun as punishment for late return.

safetyRules.title: Refer beyond training education scope
safetyRules.rule: Aggression, severe fear, sudden unexplained behaviour change, or suspected pain/illness require veterinary and/or clinical behaviour referral—not generic app protocols alone.
safetyRules.referralText: Contact veterinarian for medical causes; seek ABTC-registered Clinical Animal Behaviourist or Veterinary Behaviourist for clinical behaviour treatment.

safetyRules.title: Do not punish warning signals without addressing cause
safetyRules.rule: Do not train owners to suppress growling or other warnings without addressing underlying fear, pain, or conflict; prioritise management and professional support.

safetyRules.title: Always supervise children and dogs
safetyRules.rule: Never leave a child alone with a dog; teach do-not-disturb contexts and gentle interaction.

safetyRules.title: Do not punish warning signals
safetyRules.rule: Do not punish growling or other warnings; remove dog from trigger and seek vet/behaviourist support.
safetyRules.referralText: Veterinary assessment and accredited animal behaviourist.

safetyRules.title: Do not recommend ABTC-listed aversive tools or methods
safetyRules.rule: Good Dog must not recommend equipment or methods on ABTC indicative aversive lists (e.g. shock, choke, prong, alpha roll).

safetyRules.title: Do not confront resource guarding with force or chase games
safetyRules.rule: Do not recommend chasing, prying items from the mouth, or punishing growls over possessions; use management, trade-up, and professional referral for guarding with aggression.
safetyRules.referralText: ABTC Clinical Animal Behaviourist for resource guarding with aggression.

supportingClaims.statement: IMDT members agree to actively provide and promote force-free training methods and reject methods or equipment that may cause physical or mental discomfort.
IMDT members agree to avoid positive punishment and negative reinforcement as tools for training dogs.
IMDT members agree to work within professional limits and refer owners to a suitable professional when needs exceed those limits.
ABTC states it does not agree with aversives being used to train animals and publishes an indicative list of aversive equipment and methods that should not be used.
If a dog ignores recall during training, Dogs Trust advises staying calm because anger or shouting can reduce willingness to return; use long line guidance or collect the dog instead of punishing.
Dogs Trust advises off-lead exercise in open spaces only when the owner is confident the dog will come back when called.
RSPCA advises owners not to join classes if techniques rely on fear, pain, choke chains, shouting or hitting.
If a dog does not always come when called, Dogs Trust advises keeping them on a long line or lead rather than relying on off-lead freedom.
RSPCA advises never leaving a child alone in the same room as a dog, even the family dog.
RSPCA advises teaching children not to approach dogs when the dog is eating, sleeping, unwell, injured, tired, or near valued items.
Blue Cross advises not punishing dogs showing defensive behaviours such as growling, because punishment may suppress warnings and increase biting risk while adding stress.
Blue Cross advises removing the dog from a worrying situation when stress signs appear (e.g. lip lick, growl, moving away) and giving a calming activity such as a chew or stuffed Kong.
ABTC's June 2024 indicative list includes electric/shock collars, choke chains/collars, and prong/pinch collars as aversive equipment that should not be used in training animals.
ABTC's indicative aversive methods list includes 'alpha roll'/pinning, hitting, hard lead jerks, and kneeing the dog as methods that should not be used.
Dogs Trust immediate reactivity guidance: increase distance until the dog relaxes, then reward with praise, food or a favourite toy; avoid telling the dog off because this can increase stress.
Dogs Trust explains that chasing a dog who has stolen an item often rewards the behaviour with a fun game; owners should not play chase for stolen items.
Dogs Trust advises ignoring safe steal-and-parade behaviour until the dog drops the item, then redirecting to a toy or chew rather than immediately grabbing the stolen object.

Dogs Trust advises owners to speak up for their dog at the vet: if the dog tenses or growls, politely but firmly ask the vet to pause, because ignoring or telling off a growling dog can make the situation worse and a dog may bite when its warnings are ignored.

Blue Cross notes that dogs usually show earlier signs of stress before defensive behaviours such as stiffening and staring, growling, showing teeth, snapping or biting, that some stress signs can also be caused by a health problem so a vet should be consulted if worried, and that aggression warrants speaking to a vet and a professional animal behaviourist.

abtcRegister.title: Find an ABTC-registered trainer
abtcRegister.body: RSPCA recommends looking for ABTC-registered animal training instructors for ethical training that meets welfare needs.

vetFirst.title: See your vet first
vetFirst.body: Dogs Trust advises having a reactive dog examined by a vet to check for underlying medical conditions before behaviour change work, noting pain and illness can reduce tolerance and coping.

dogsTrustBehaviourLine.title: Dogs Trust Behaviour Support Line
dogsTrustBehaviourLine.body: Free telephone advice for UK dog owners struggling with behaviour.

professionalRoles.statement: RSPCA recommends looking for ABTC-registered animal training instructors for ethical training that meets welfare needs.

BVA abnormal behaviour policy states that pain, illness, and discomfort can contribute to behavioural signs and that veterinary assessment should be considered when behaviour changes or abnormal behaviour is suspected.

ABTC registers distinct practitioner roles (including training instructors and clinical animal behaviourists); KindTrail paraphrases that training instructors teach skills and management while complex behaviour cases should involve ABTC-registered clinical behaviourists and veterinary input—see existing claim-rspca-003-abtc-trainer and src-abtc-owners.

assessmentMetrics.title: Name response within 2 seconds
assessmentMetrics.observableCriteria: Dog orients to handler within 2 seconds of name spoken once at conversational volume.

assessmentMetrics.title: Recall on long line — 5 metres
assessmentMetrics.observableCriteria: Single recall cue; dog returns to within arm's reach on 5m long line in low distraction.

assessmentMetrics.title: Recall on long line — 10 metres
assessmentMetrics.observableCriteria: Single recall cue; reliable on 10m long line with mild distraction.

assessmentMetrics.title: Loose lead — 10 consecutive steps
assessmentMetrics.observableCriteria: Ten consecutive steps with slack lead without owner stopping.

assessmentMetrics.title: Off-lead freedom (not auto-unlocked)
assessmentMetrics.observableCriteria: App must not promote off-lead in public until tier 2 recall met AND owner confirms secure area or professional sign-off.

Blue Cross advises not punishing dogs showing defensive behaviours such as growling, because punishment may suppress warnings and increase biting risk while adding stress.

Dogs Trust advises teaching reliable name response before adding a formal recall cue.

lesson.title: Introduce a marker word
lesson.summary: Teach your dog that a calm 'yes' (or click) always means a reward is coming, before learning new skills.

protocol.title: Charge a marker signal (Dogs Trust pattern)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog shows clear anticipation (orientation toward handler/treats) immediately after marker with no behaviour requirement.

steps.instruction: Choose one marker (calm verbal word such as 'yes', clicker, whistle, or visual signal for deaf dogs) and use it consistently in tone and form.
steps.rewardTiming: Deliver treat immediately after each marker.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog orients toward handler or treats within one second of marker on repeated trials.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use higher-value treats; reduce environmental stimulation; increase distance from distractions.
failureModes: Marker word used in daily speech causing confusion

steps.instruction: Repeat marker then treat pairing multiple times in a short session until dog visibly anticipates food after the marker alone.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat within 1–2 seconds of marker on every repetition during charging phase.
steps.progressCriteria: Anticipatory response to marker without requiring body movement cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten sessions; pause if dog disengages.
failureModes: Gaps between marker and treat too long

steps.instruction: Begin teaching new behaviours only after charging criterion met; maintain rule that marker is always followed by reward during learning phase.
steps.rewardTiming: Marker marks exact behaviour instant; reward follows immediately.
steps.progressCriteria: Stable anticipation across at least two sessions.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Re-charge marker in easier environment if anticipation fades.

safetyPrecautions: Do not train on full stomach if dog prone to vomiting with excitement—adjust timing

claims.statement: A marker signal must always be followed by a reward so the dog can be confident they got the behaviour right.
Before training new behaviours, the dog should learn that the marker predicts a reward via repeated marker-then-treat pairings.
Dogs Trust advises saying a verbal marker as calmly as possible because excited delivery can excite, confuse or distract the dog.

lesson.title: First sit with a lure
lesson.summary: Use a treat lure, reward the moment your dog sits, then add the word 'sit' at the right time.

protocol.title: Teach sit with food lure (RSPCA six-step outline)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog sits on verbal cue 'sit' with hindquarters on ground.

steps.instruction: With dog standing, hold treat near nose.
steps.rewardTiming: No reward until sit occurs in later steps.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog tracks treat with nose.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use smellier treat; shorten sessions.
failureModes: Lure held too high causing jump

steps.instruction: Move hand in arc over head so dog follows treat; as head rises, bottom goes to floor; praise and treat the instant sit happens.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat immediately on sit.
steps.progressCriteria: Bottom contacts floor following lure arc.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Smaller arc; reward partial sits only if shaping intentionally.
failureModes: Backing up instead of sitting—train with wall behind

steps.instruction: Practice in short regular sessions.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat each successful sit during acquisition.
steps.progressCriteria: Repeated sits with lure.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Fewer reps per session.

steps.instruction: Add verbal cue 'sit' as dog moves into sit, not before movement.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat on completed sit after cue timed correctly.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog sits when lure used with correctly timed verbal cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Delay adding verbal cue until lure reliable.

steps.instruction: Continue short regular practice.
steps.rewardTiming: Maintain reinforcement for correct sits.
steps.progressCriteria: Sit begins without excessive lure dependence.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Fade lure gradually—not specified numerically by RSPCA.

steps.instruction: Use an 'okay' or release cue to mark end of exercise.
steps.rewardTiming: Optional release reward per owner choice.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog waits until release after sit when trained for duration separately.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Keep duration short initially.

claims.statement: RSPCA recommends breaking training into short but regular sessions and starting new tricks in a quiet room with minimal distractions.
RSPCA advises adding the verbal cue 'sit' only as the dog moves into sit, not before, to avoid associating the word with the wrong movement.

lesson.title: Teach down without forcing
lesson.summary: Lure or shape a down and never push your dog into position.

protocol.title: Lie down with lure and shaping (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog lies down on verbal 'down' cue.

steps.instruction: From sit, lure hand toward floor in front of paws; mark and reward any down or shaping step toward floor.
steps.rewardTiming: Mark at elbows on floor or closest approximation.
steps.progressCriteria: Full down with lure.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reward head dip or elbow bend only until full down emerges.

steps.instruction: Fade visible lure; add verbal 'down' before gesture once behaviour reliable.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward completed down.
steps.progressCriteria: Down on verbal cue with minimal gesture.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reintroduce brief lure.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust instructs owners never to push a dog's back down to force a down; use luring/shaping and reward instead.

lesson.title: Build name response
lesson.summary: Reward check-ins, then teach your dog that their name means look at you—without repeating it.

protocol.title: Name response and attention (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog orients to handler promptly when name is spoken once.

steps.instruction: Reward every voluntary glance toward handler without saying name yet.
steps.rewardTiming: Immediate treat on glance.
steps.progressCriteria: Frequent check-ins.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Higher value treats.
failureModes: Only rewarding when dog is naughty

steps.instruction: Say name once; when dog looks, throw treat to side; repeat varying direction; generalise locations.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat after orientation.
steps.progressCriteria: Reliable name response in moderate distraction.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Do not repeat name; move slightly to prompt.

lesson.title: Settle on a mat
lesson.summary: Help your dog choose calm on a blanket, with more relaxation rewarded over time.

protocol.title: Settle on mat (Dogs Trust relaxation training)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog voluntarily relaxes on blanket/mat with increasing duration and distractions.

steps.instruction: Sit quietly; drop treats on mat for any behaviour that is not staring, pulling, or barking; gradually reinforce lie down and relaxation signs.
steps.rewardTiming: Quiet delivery of treats onto mat.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog chooses mat and shows relaxed posture.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reward standing quietly or sniffing blanket first.
failureModes: Talking or commanding repeatedly during settle

steps.instruction: Increase duration between treats; add distractions at distance; if dog gets up, wait for re-settle before rewarding.
steps.rewardTiming: After sustained calm.
steps.progressCriteria: Settle with mild distractions indoors/outdoors.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Increase distance from distraction.

lesson.title: Build a stay
lesson.summary: Reward your dog in position, return before treating, and build duration before distance.

protocol.title: Stay — duration, distance and distraction (Dogs Trust)
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog remains in sit/down until handler returns and rewards in position.

steps.instruction: Build sit duration beside dog; add single 'stay' cue; return before rewarding; reward only in position.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat while dog still in stay.
steps.progressCriteria: 10s stay with unpredictable duration pattern before reward.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorter durations; end session on success.

steps.instruction: Add lean/step away and return; gradually vary direction and distance; generalise locations with higher value treats.
steps.rewardTiming: Always after returning to dog.
steps.progressCriteria: Stay with moderate distance and distractions.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reset to shorter stay in new location.

lesson.title: Leave it — foundations
lesson.summary: Teach your dog to look away from tempting items and wait for a better reward.

protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog orientates away from presented item on 'leave' cue without taking it.

steps.instruction: Hold low-value item in one hand; when dog sniffs then looks or moves away, mark and reward from other hand with better treat.
steps.rewardTiming: Mark at look-away; treat immediately.
steps.progressCriteria: Reliable look-away before cue added.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use more boring decoy item; higher-value reward.

steps.rewardTiming: On successful leave response.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog looks away on cue before item reachable.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Increase distance to item.

steps.rewardTiming: Maintain high-value reward for difficult leaves.
steps.progressCriteria: Success in moderate distraction environments.

lesson.title: Stop when the lead tightens
lesson.summary: Help your dog learn that a loose lead keeps the walk moving.

protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog walks with slack lead; forward motion contingent on loose lead.

lesson.title: Socialise your puppy safely

protocol.intendedOutcome: Puppy forms positive associations with everyday people, animals, sounds, surfaces and objects during the early socialisation window.

lesson.title: Read stress signals
lesson.summary: Notice lip licks, yawning, and turning away—pause and help your dog feel safe.

protocol.title: Recognise and respond to stress signals
protocol.intendedOutcome: Owner notices early stress signs in context, calmly gives the dog space, and knows when to involve a vet or behaviourist.

steps.instruction: Look at your dog as a whole, together with the situation, not just one sign. Subtle signs include yawning when not tired, lip licking, panting when not hot, pinned-back ears, whale eye, pacing, and turning away or withdrawing. Clearer signs include loss of appetite, backing away, a tucked tail, cowering, trembling and a fixed stare.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable; observation step.
steps.progressCriteria: Owner can name at least two stress signs their dog shows and what was happening at the time.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Note down when and where the signs happen to spot a pattern.
failureModes: Relying on a single sign out of context

steps.instruction: When you see stress signs, stay calm, avoid raising your voice, and move your dog away from the cause or give them a quiet space to retreat to without forcing interaction.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable; no reward is needed to allow a break.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog settles or recovers once the stressor is removed.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Increase the distance or end the activity for the day.
failureModes: Telling the dog off for growling or backing away

steps.instruction: Keep routines steady, change them gradually, and balance enrichment with plenty of rest. Contact your vet if the change in behaviour is sudden, or if signs keep happening, because health problems can cause similar signs.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable.
steps.progressCriteria: Stress signs become less frequent, or the owner has a vet appointment booked.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Ask your vet for tailored advice or a referral.
failureModes: Assuming a sudden change is only a training problem

referralRequirements: Your vet, then an ABTC-registered clinical animal behaviourist if there is aggression or persistent fear.

claims.statement: Blue Cross advises not punishing dogs showing defensive behaviours such as growling, because punishment may suppress warnings and increase biting risk while adding stress.
Blue Cross stress guidance (batch 002 source) lists lip licking, yawning, pinned ears, and turning away as stress signs owners should notice before escalation.

Blue Cross lists subtle stress signs as yawning when not tired, panting with a curled tongue tip, pacing, lip licking, pinned-back ears, dilated pupils or red eyes and whale eye, and obvious signs as loss of appetite, backing away, tucked tail, cowering, diarrhoea or increased bowel movements, and trembling when not cold or excited.

Blue Cross notes that dogs usually show earlier signs of stress before defensive behaviours such as stiffening and staring, growling, showing teeth, snapping or biting, that some stress signs can also be caused by a health problem so a vet should be consulted if worried, and that aggression warrants speaking to a vet and a professional animal behaviourist.

Blue Cross suggests helping a stressed dog by removing it from the stressful situation or giving it a quiet separate space, staying calm without raising your voice, providing indoor entertainment and walks, and not telling the dog off.

PDSA advises reading a dog's body language as a whole, together with the situation, rather than relying on one sign; stress signs it lists include yawning when not tired, nose or lip licking, a low or tucked tail, panting when not warm, pinned-back ears, stiff body, whale eye, withdrawing or turning away when approached, not eating, low energy and a fixed stare.

PDSA advises noticing patterns in when stress occurs (at home, on walks, around other dogs, when left alone), contacting a vet if behaviour changes suddenly, removing a scared dog from the situation without forcing interaction, keeping routines and changing them gradually, giving a quiet safe space others do not disturb, balancing enrichment with rest, and using reward-based training instead of punishment.

protocol.title: Get your dog comfortable with handling and vet visits
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog accepts gentle handling at home and has positive experiences of the vet clinic before a procedure is needed.

steps.instruction: When you and your dog are both relaxed, touch a part of the body your dog already enjoys being touched for no more than three seconds, then give a treat. Keep sessions short and frequent.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat just after each touch.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog stays relaxed and stays with you for several touches in a row.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten the touch or go back to a more comfortable area.

steps.instruction: Slowly move to new areas, always in the same order, and use a cue such as 'let me see' before touching. Work towards paws, tail, ears and mouth, and build touch time gradually from three to ten seconds. Stop if your dog seems uncomfortable.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat after each touch.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog accepts touch on each area for up to ten seconds while staying relaxed.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Go back to the last area where your dog was relaxed and progress more slowly.

steps.instruction: Practise in new quiet places and with other people, starting again from a gentle fuss each time. Drop in at the vet for treats and a fuss between appointments if your dog enjoys it, and bring a favourite toy or blanket.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat for calm behaviour at each new place.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog stays relaxed being handled in a new place by a familiar person.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Make visits shorter and quieter, and go at your dog's pace.
failureModes: Skipping back to full handling in a new place

referralRequirements: Your vet first to rule out pain, then an accredited behaviourist via your vet if your dog still dislikes being handled.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises introducing handling gradually in short, frequent sessions in a quiet familiar place, only when owner and dog are both relaxed, starting where the dog already enjoys touch, and stopping if the dog seems uncomfortable.

Dogs Trust advises giving a treat just after touching each body part, handling in the same order each time so the dog can predict what happens, using a verbal cue such as 'let me see', then repeating the process in new quiet locations and with new people, going back to the beginning each time.

Dogs Trust advises that a dog with an established fear of handling, or who shows signs of aggression when handled, should be seen by a vet because pain makes fear and aggressive responses more likely; if the dog is well, the vet can refer to an accredited behaviourist.

Dogs Trust recommends 'touch and treat' practice at home before vet visits: touch a comfortable area for no more than three seconds then treat, move to a new area only gradually, stop if the dog looks uncomfortable, and slowly build touch time from three to ten seconds, working towards paws, tail and mouth.

Dogs Trust advises owners to speak up for their dog at the vet: if the dog tenses or growls, politely but firmly ask the vet to pause, because ignoring or telling off a growling dog can make the situation worse and a dog may bite when its warnings are ignored.

Dogs Trust suggests dropping in at the vet clinic for treats and a fuss when no procedure is needed (if the dog enjoys it), bringing a favourite toy or blanket, sitting away from the door, facing the dog away from other dogs, and encouraging focus on the owner in the waiting room.

lesson.title: How dogs learn: rewards, markers and associations
lesson.summary: Dogs repeat what pays off and link events that happen together, so reward the behaviour you want straight away and check what your dog is already being rewarded for.

protocol.title: Use rewards so your dog learns clearly
protocol.intendedOutcome: Owner picks rewards the dog really wants, delivers them straight away, and understands that behaviour followed by a reward is likely to be repeated.

steps.instruction: Find rewards your dog really wants. Most dogs like food, toys and your attention, and some like a favourite game or a sniff. Use soft, smelly treats cut pea-sized for hard moments and plain biscuits for easy practice.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward straight after the behaviour.
steps.progressCriteria: You can name a top reward and an everyday reward for your dog.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Offer a few options and watch which your dog works for.
failureModes: Using a reward the dog does not actually want

steps.instruction: Give the reward during the behaviour or within about half a second afterwards so your dog links the two. If you use a marker such as 'yes' or a click, say it calmly at the right moment and always follow it with a reward, repeating the pairing around 20 times at the start.
steps.rewardTiming: Marker, then reward straight away.
steps.progressCriteria: Your dog looks for the reward when it hears the marker.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Practise the marker-then-treat pairing for longer before asking for anything.
failureModes: Marker with no reward after it

steps.instruction: When teaching something new, reward every success. Once your dog does it well in different places, reward every other time, then less often, mixing treats with praise and a fuss so your dog stays interested.
steps.rewardTiming: Every time at first, then thin out.
steps.progressCriteria: Your dog still tries hard when rewards come less often.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Go back to rewarding every time if your dog stops trying.

steps.instruction: Check what your dog is already being rewarded for. Attention, eye contact and being pushed away can all be rewards, so unwanted behaviour may continue even when you are telling the dog off. Ask for a calm behaviour and reward that instead.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward the calm choice you want.
steps.progressCriteria: You can spot one thing your dog does for attention and what you now reward instead.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Pick one behaviour to watch for a day.
failureModes: Giving attention to the behaviour you want to stop

steps.instruction: Keep it kind and clear: end each short session on a success, teach one cue at a time with short consistent words, ignore mistakes and reward the next correct try, and make sure everyone at home uses the same cues. Never shout at, hit or frighten your dog.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward the next correct try.
steps.progressCriteria: Sessions end on a success and everyone uses the same cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten the session and make the task easier.
failureModes: Telling the dog off for mistakes
Different family members using different words

referralRequirements: Your vet, then an ABTC-registered behaviourist if the dog shows fear or aggression.

claims.statement: Positive reinforcement training means giving the dog something they want when they behave in a way the owner likes, making that behaviour more likely in future.
When starting a new skill, Dogs Trust advises rewarding the dog every time they are successful; reward type and schedule can change after the behaviour is reliable across environments.
A marker signal must always be followed by a reward so the dog can be confident they got the behaviour right.
Undesired behaviour may increase if the dog receives attention, eye contact or interaction as a consequence—even when the owner intends to discourage the behaviour.
Before training new behaviours, the dog should learn that the marker predicts a reward via repeated marker-then-treat pairings.
Dogs Trust advises saying a verbal marker as calmly as possible because excited delivery can excite, confuse or distract the dog.

Blue Cross says dogs learn by association: when a dog does something and is rewarded straight afterwards, the action is much more likely to be repeated, and once the dog understands the request the owner can pair it with a cue such as 'sit'.

Blue Cross teaches a reward marker by saying 'yes', clicking or giving a thumbs-up for a deaf dog and giving a treat straight afterwards, repeated around 20 times, and says the marker should not replace the reward.
PDSA says the reward should be given during the behaviour or within half a second after it so the dog links the two.

PDSA's golden rules include choosing a reward the dog really likes, keeping sessions short and ending on a success, teaching one command at a time with short, consistent commands, ignoring mistakes and rewarding the next correct attempt, and getting everyone to use the same commands.

PDSA says punishment such as shouting, smacking, water pistols, rattle cans and choke chains causes anxiety and fear, makes learning slower, and can lead to behaviour problems later, and that dogs do not need an owner who acts as a dominant 'pack leader'.

Dogs Trust advises using soft, smelly high-value treats as a 'gold star' reward and when there are more distractions, using less exciting treats for easy practice, and picking something extra tempting when a busier place makes responding hard.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust recommends swapping items a dog should not have for something better ('fair trade') so the dog willingly releases items rather than guarding them.
Dogs Trust explains that chasing a dog who has stolen an item often rewards the behaviour with a fun game; owners should not play chase for stolen items.
Dogs Trust advises ignoring safe steal-and-parade behaviour until the dog drops the item, then redirecting to a toy or chew rather than immediately grabbing the stolen object.

Dogs Trust teaches fair trade by letting the dog play with a not-favourite toy for a few seconds, placing a handful of very tasty treats beside the dog so the dog chooses to move to the food, rewarding that choice, letting the dog play with the toy again, and adding a cue such as 'drop' only once the dog is reliably letting go.

lesson.title: Teach your dog to spin
lesson.summary: Lure your dog's nose in a circle, reward half turns, then add the word and a small hand signal in short, fun sessions.

protocol.title: Teach your dog to spin
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog turns a full circle on the word 'spin' with a small hand signal.

steps.instruction: Have your dog stand in front of you. Hold a treat at its nose and slowly move it to the side of its head so it follows with its nose.
steps.rewardTiming: Mark and reward when the dog has followed the lure.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog follows the treat round to the side.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reward any small turn.

steps.instruction: Keep moving the treat in a circle around your dog's body. When it finishes a circle, mark with an enthusiastic 'yes' and give the treat. If it struggles, reward a half turn first, then build to a full circle.
steps.rewardTiming: Mark at the end of the circle.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog turns a full circle confidently.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Go back to rewarding half turns.
failureModes: Rewarding only when the dog has already lost interest

steps.instruction: Add the word 'spin' as you guide your dog round with an empty hand, then make the hand signal smaller until you are just moving your wrist and pointing.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward after the full circle.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog spins on the word and small signal.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Go back to the previous step if your dog is unsure.
failureModes: Using a big signal for too long

referralRequirements: Your vet if your dog seems stiff or sore when turning.

claims.statement: Blue Cross teaches a spin by luring the dog's nose from in front, round to the side and in a circle around its body, marking and rewarding a full circle, and rewarding smaller movements such as a half turn first if the dog struggles.
Blue Cross adds the word 'spin' and a hand signal by guiding the dog round with an empty hand, then making the signal smaller; if the dog is unsure, go back to the previous step.
Blue Cross advises spin sessions of up to five minutes in a low-distraction area, and to stop and give the dog space if it shows frustration such as barking, whining, mouthing, pawing or jumping up.

lesson.title: Kind equipment and the legal basics
lesson.summary: Use a collar with an ID tag, a well-fitted harness and rewards; avoid prong, choke and shock devices, and check the current rules.

protocol.title: Choose kind equipment and meet the legal basics
protocol.intendedOutcome: Dog wears a well-fitted harness and collar with ID tag comfortably, and the owner avoids pain-based equipment.

steps.instruction: Put a collar with an identity tag on your dog and keep it on in public even if you walk in a harness. Make sure the microchip details are up to date.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable.
steps.progressCriteria: Collar and tag fitted and microchip details checked.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Ask your vet to check the microchip.
failureModes: Taking the collar off in public

steps.instruction: Choose a harness that does not cross directly over the shoulders and restrict movement. It should fit so you can slip a finger between strap and body and your dog cannot slip out. Check collar, harness and lead for wear regularly.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable.
steps.progressCriteria: You can pass the one-finger and slip-out checks.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Ask a pet shop or your vet to help with fit.

steps.instruction: Introduce the harness slowly. Scatter treats around it, feed treats through the head hole, rest it loosely on the neck, let your dog hear the clips, then fasten it with treats. Go back a stage if your dog worries.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat at each small step.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog wears the harness relaxed indoors.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Stay longer on the previous stage or stop for the day.

steps.instruction: Keep to equipment that does not hurt or frighten. Prong collars, choke chains and shock collars rely on pain or fear, and welfare charities and vets advise against them. Teach loose lead walking with rewards instead, and check current rules because they are under review in England.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward walking close by with treats.
steps.progressCriteria: You walk using only the harness or flat collar and food rewards.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Ask a qualified reward-based trainer to help.

referralRequirements: Your vet first, then an accredited behaviourist if your dog is fearful of handling.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust states that equipment promising to 'cure' pulling by causing pain or discomfort in sensitive areas is unnecessary and can be unpleasant and confusing for dogs; flat collar or comfortable harness is preferred.
GOV.UK states all dogs in the UK must be microchipped and registered on an approved database by 8 weeks old.

Dogs Trust advises choosing a harness that does not cross directly over the shoulders and restrict movement, that fits so a finger can slip between the strapping and the body, and that the dog cannot slip out of; it also advises checking harness, collar and lead regularly for wear.

Dogs Trust introduces a harness in small steps: treats scattered around it, feeding treats through the head hole, resting it loosely on the neck, getting the dog used to the clip sounds, then doing it up with treats, and going back a stage or stopping if the dog worries.

The RSPCA says prong collars work by causing pain or discomfort, can cause injury and new behaviour problems such as fear and aggression, and do not teach positive behaviour; its head of behaviour, a vet, says she would never recommend them for training.
The RSPCA notes that prong collars are not illegal in the UK although it wants them banned, and recommends a well-fitting, comfortable harness plus teaching loose lead walking with food.
The Dog Ownership Guide says by law a dog in public must wear a collar with an identity tag even when walked in a harness, and that microchip details must be kept up to date.

The BVA says electric shock collars are banned in Wales (2010 regulations), that the Scottish Government has said aversive devices including electric collars may be an offence of causing unnecessary suffering, that Northern Ireland has no specific law, and that in England the government has been working towards a ban rather than having one in force.

The BVA says even low-level electric shock produces stress, pain and fear responses in dogs and cats, lists choke collars, prong collars and anti-bark collars as other aversive devices of concern, and recommends reward-based training.
In a written answer on 27 May 2026 a Defra minister said Defra will consult on whether to ban electric shock collars later in this Parliament, with next steps to be announced in due course.

lesson.title: Plan short sessions and track progress
lesson.summary: Practise one skill at a time for a few minutes, add distraction slowly and keep a simple diary to see what is working.

protocol.title: Plan short sessions and track progress
protocol.intendedOutcome: Owner practises one skill at a time in short sessions, adds distractions gradually and keeps a simple diary so progress is visible.

steps.instruction: Pick one skill at a time and keep sessions short, about two to five minutes, practising little and often. Stop on a success.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward every success at the start.
steps.progressCriteria: You manage several short sessions in a week.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Cut the session shorter.
failureModes: Long sessions that end in frustration

steps.instruction: Start in a quiet place with few distractions, then move to places with more distraction only when your dog copes. If it cannot focus, go back to the earlier place for a while.
steps.rewardTiming: Use better rewards when distraction goes up.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog copes in a new, mildly distracting place.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Return to the quiet place.
failureModes: Adding a new place and a new distraction at the same time

steps.instruction: Keep a simple diary. For each session write the date, skill, place, distractions, reward used and how it went. It shows progress and helps if you need to ask a trainer for help.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable.
steps.progressCriteria: You can see which skills work in which places.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use a note on your phone.
failureModes: Not writing the place and distraction

steps.instruction: Look back after a week or two. If a skill works at home but not outside, practise it in the in-between places. Ask a qualified trainer or your vet if progress stalls or your dog shows fear or aggression.
steps.rewardTiming: Not applicable.
steps.progressCriteria: You choose the next skill or place from your diary.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Ask a reward-based trainer to review your diary.

referralRequirements: Your vet and an accredited behaviourist if fear or aggression are involved.

claims.statement: Blue Cross advises keeping training sessions short (about two to five minutes), practising little and often, and practising in different places while keeping distractions to a minimum in the early stages of learning.

PDSA's golden rules include choosing a reward the dog really likes, keeping sessions short and ending on a success, teaching one command at a time with short, consistent commands, ignoring mistakes and rewarding the next correct attempt, and getting everyone to use the same commands.

An RSPCA branch suggests training little and often, such as three to four sessions a week of five to fifteen minutes, starting in low-distraction places and moving to higher distraction only once the dog copes, going back if the dog cannot focus, and keeping a training diary to track progress and help with troubleshooting.
